en.note:
The idea

Many Dutch verbs are made of a particle + a verb: op + staan = opstaan (to get up), mee + gaan = meegaan (to go along, to come along). They are a lot like English phrasal verbs such as "get up", "call up" or "come back", where a little word changes the meaning of the verb. The twist is that in Dutch, in a main clause, these two parts split up, and the particle travels much further than in English.

The rule: the particle goes to the end

In the present tense the conjugated verb stays in second position as always, while the particle goes to the very end of the sentence. This creates the same "frame" you saw with modal verbs.

infinitivesentenceEnglish
opstaanIk sta om zeven uur op.I get up at seven.
opbellenHij belt zijn moeder op.He calls his mother (up).
aankomenDe trein komt om tien uur aan.The train arrives at ten.
uitgaanWe gaan vanavond uit.We're going out tonight.
meegaanGa je mee?Are you coming (with us)?

With inversion and in questions, too, the particle stays at the end: Morgen kom ik terug. Hoe laat kom je aan?

With a modal: the verb stays in one piece

When there is a modal verb (unit 9), the separable verb is an infinitive at the end of the sentence, so it stays together: Ik moet morgen vroeg opstaan. Wil je vanavond uitgaan?

The most common particles

op (up, on), mee (along, with), aan (on, at), uit (out), terug (back), binnen (in, inside). You can also recognize them by the stress: in separable verbs the stress falls on the particle: ÓPstaan, MÉEgaan, teRUGkomen.

Prefixes that never split

Verbs starting with be-, ver-, ont-, her- (and also ge-, er-) are inseparable: the prefix always stays attached and the stress falls on the verb, not the prefix, just like English "beCOME" or "forGET" (Dutch vergeten).

infinitivesentence
betalen (to pay)Ik betaal de koffie.
vertellen (to tell)Hij vertelt het aan zijn zus.
ontmoeten (to meet)Ik ontmoet Sofie vanavond.
herhalen (to repeat)Kunt u dat herhalen?
begrijpen (to understand)Ik begrijp het niet.

In unit 19 you'll see that separable verbs also behave in a special way in the past participle.

Watch out: typical mistakes for English speakers

  • Keeping the verb together in the present: Ik opsta om zeven uur → Ik sta om zeven uur op.
  • Putting the particle right after the verb, as in "call up your mother": Hij belt op zijn moeder → Hij belt zijn moeder op.
  • Stopping the particle too early in a long sentence: in Dutch it goes after time, place and everything else: Ik sta morgen om zeven uur op.
  • Splitting the verb after a modal: Ik moet sta op → Ik moet opstaan.
  • Splitting an inseparable verb: Ik taal de koffie be → Ik betaal de koffie.
en.vlaams: In Belgium you often hear buitengaan for "to go outside": "Ik ga buiten" (I'm going outside). In the Netherlands people tend to say naar buiten gaan. uitgaan, on the other hand, means "to go out (in the evening), to have fun" everywhere.

hard.q: Waarom ga je zaterdag niet met ons ___?
hard.e: Trap: even though met ons is already there, the verb is meegaan, so the particle mee still goes at the end. Met on its own can't end the sentence (unlike English "come with").

g.samen: together: the particle of meegaan is missing
